scenes.visual: Title card 'Floors and Brackets' over a cut-away stack of rock layers with a FLAG and a GOLD bracket. COLOUR MAP, same in both films: GREEN = speciation (lambda, new branches); RED = extinction (mu, branches ending); NAVY = surviving lineages; GREY with a cross = extinct lineages; GOLD = iridium band and the bracket between two dated ash layers; a FLAG with a downward arrow = a fossil floor, labelled 'by this time, at the latest'. Time runs left to right toward 'Today'. Cream background, 16:9. Every number appears only as on-screen text. Organisms and rocks are simple cartoons; anything not computed is labelled 'schematic'. In this film: NAVY dots = uranium (parent) atoms; GREY dots = lead (daughter) atoms.

scenes.tts: The first film put dates on its fossil flags and on the last cliff. But how can a rock say when a bone was buried, with no one there to see?
scenes.visual: Brief recap: the first film's timeline with its flags and the end-Cretaceous drop labelled '66 Ma'. It tilts and sinks into a vertical column of rock layers, a cartoon bone in one layer, a question mark beside it.
scenes.narration: The first film put dates on its fossil flags and on the last cliff. But how can a rock say when a bone was buried, with no one there to see?

scenes.tts: Fossils are rarely dated directly. Often, minerals in the rocks around them are. A favourite is zircon. It crystallizes in molten rock, and an eruption carries it into volcanic ash.
scenes.visual: A cut-away volcano: small crystals form in the magma chamber, one labelled 'zircon'. An eruption carries them up and drops a thin ash layer onto the column. Zoom into the ash: the zircon sits among the ash grains. Label 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Fossils are rarely dated directly. Often, minerals in the rocks around them are. A favourite is zircon. It crystallizes in molten rock, and an eruption carries it into volcanic ash.

scenes.tts: As zircon crystallizes, it takes up uranium but almost no lead. So nearly all the lead inside it comes from later decay.
scenes.visual: The zircon crystal grows; inside it a 4-by-4 grid of 16 NAVY dots, label 'uranium (parent)'. A few GREY dots try to enter and bounce off, label 'almost no lead at the start'.
scenes.narration: As zircon crystallizes, it takes up uranium but almost no lead. So nearly all the lead inside it comes from later decay.

scenes.tts: Each uranium atom has the same small chance of decaying in any given year. So half the parent atoms decay in a fixed time, the half-life. It is constant for each isotope.
scenes.visual: A clock face labelled 'one half-life' sweeps once; on screen the definition 'half-life = time for half the parent atoms to decay'. A small curve sketches the parent amount falling steeply, then more slowly, label 'not a straight line'.
scenes.narration: Each uranium atom has the same small chance of decaying in any given year. So half the parent atoms decay in a fixed time, the half-life. It is constant for each isotope.

scenes.tts: Watch the grid. On average, after one half-life, half the uranium has become lead. After the next, half of what was left. The crystal keeps time from the moment it formed.
scenes.visual: The 16-dot grid: with each sweep of the clock, about half the remaining NAVY dots flip to GREY at scattered, random positions (16 navy, then 8, then 4), counted on screen only as dots, no fractions. Small label 'illustrative averages: each atom decays at random'. An hourglass icon turns over at the start, label 'started when the crystal formed'.
scenes.narration: Watch the grid. On average, after one half-life, half the uranium has become lead. After the next, half of what was left. The crystal keeps time from the moment it formed.

scenes.tts: Suppose the crystal stayed closed and started with no lead. Then the parent left and the lead built up count the half-lives. That count gives the age.
scenes.visual: A cartoon instrument labelled 'measure parent and daughter' reads the grid; a small seal on the crystal labelled 'closed: nothing in or out' and a tag 'no lead at the start'. A counter labelled 'half-lives passed' appears beside it, then an arrow to 'age'. No numbers.
scenes.narration: Suppose the crystal stayed closed and started with no lead. Then the parent left and the lead built up count the half-lives. That count gives the age.

scenes.tts: Now take a stack of rock layers. A bed of fossils lies between two layers of volcanic ash. Each ash can be dated by its zircons.
scenes.visual: The rock column returns: ash layer at top labelled 'ash above', a fossil bed with shells in the middle, ash layer below labelled 'ash below'. A small zircon icon pulses in each ash.
scenes.narration: Now take a stack of rock layers. A bed of fossils lies between two layers of volcanic ash. Each ash can be dated by its zircons.

scenes.tts: In undisturbed layers, younger ones settle on top of older ones. So the oldest lies at the bottom. How old, then, are the fossils between the two ashes?
scenes.visual: Arrows show layers settling one on top of another, label 'undisturbed: oldest at the bottom'. A question mark sits on the fossil bed.
scenes.narration: In undisturbed layers, younger ones settle on top of older ones. So the oldest lies at the bottom. How old, then, are the fossils between the two ashes?

scenes.visual: Hold the column; a 5-second countdown; caption 'Predict: how old is the fossil bed?'

scenes.tts: Younger than the ash below, and older than the ash above. The answer is a bracket, not a single date.
scenes.visual: A GOLD bracket snaps from the lower ash to the upper ash, enclosing the fossil bed; labels 'older than this' at the top ash and 'younger than this' at the bottom ash. Banner 'a bracket, not a point'.
scenes.narration: Younger than the ash below, and older than the ash above. The answer is a bracket, not a single date.

scenes.tts: Now look at the oldest known fossil of a group. It shows the group was here by then. It does not show when the group began.
scenes.visual: Slide down the column to the lowest layer holding a shell of one kind. A FLAG plants there with its downward arrow, label 'oldest known fossil'.
scenes.narration: Now look at the oldest known fossil of a group. It shows the group was here by then. It does not show when the group began.

scenes.tts: Earlier members may never have been preserved, or may not have been found yet. So a first fossil is a floor, a minimum age. The group may be older.
scenes.visual: Below the flag, faded ghost shells appear in older layers, label 'not preserved or not yet found'. The flag's label changes to 'minimum age: by this time, at the latest'.
scenes.narration: Earlier members may never have been preserved, or may not have been found yet. So a first fossil is a floor, a minimum age. The group may be older.

scenes.tts: Oxygen in the air is a different kind of date. The start of the Great Oxidation Event was bracketed by dated volcanic rocks, from both sides.
scenes.visual: The first film's shaded oxygen band returns, with GOLD brackets at both ends anchored on volcanic rock layers, label 'onset bracketed from both sides'.
scenes.narration: Oxygen in the air is a different kind of date. The start of the Great Oxidation Event was bracketed by dated volcanic rocks, from both sides.

scenes.tts: The clock must also fit the age. Carbon fourteen decays quickly. Long before the age of dinosaurs, too little is left to measure.
scenes.caption: The clock must also fit the age. Carbon-14 decays quickly. Long before the age of dinosaurs, too little is left to measure.
scenes.visual: A second, small hourglass labelled 'carbon-14, half-life about 5,730 years' runs out fast; a bar marks '~50,000 years: too little left'. Beside it, the uranium hourglass, labelled 'uranium-235 to lead-207', barely moves.
scenes.narration: The clock must also fit the age. Carbon-14 decays quickly. Long before the age of dinosaurs, too little is left to measure.

scenes.tts: So dinosaur bones are not carbon dated. Where volcanic ash lies near them, slower clocks date those layers. Elsewhere, other methods tie the rocks to dated layers.
scenes.caption: So dinosaur bones are not carbon-dated. Where volcanic ash lies near them, slower clocks date those layers. Elsewhere, other methods tie the rocks to dated layers.
scenes.visual: A cartoon dinosaur bone with a red 'no carbon-14' stamp; arrows point to ash layers above and below it with zircon icons, label 'where ash occurs'. A second, ash-free column beside it is linked by a dashed line to a dated column, label 'other methods'.
scenes.narration: So dinosaur bones are not carbon-dated. Where volcanic ash lies near them, slower clocks date those layers. Elsewhere, other methods tie the rocks to dated layers.

scenes.tts: Two kinds of date run through this lesson. Dated layers around a fossil give a bracket. A group's oldest known fossil gives a floor.
scenes.visual: Split screen: left, the GOLD bracket around a fossil bed between two dated layers; right, the FLAG with its downward arrow. Labels 'bracket' and 'floor'.
scenes.narration: Two kinds of date run through this lesson. Dated layers around a fossil give a bracket. A group's oldest known fossil gives a floor.

scenes.visual: Hex end card. Take-home line: 'Dated layers give a bracket; a first fossil gives a floor.'
